title: Spokane Wildfires Destroy Over 700 Buildings, Force 65,000 to Evacuate in Washington's Worst Natural Disaster
excerpt: Three blazes burning on the outskirts of Washington's second-largest city remain at 0% containment as officials describe devastated neighborhoods as a 'war zone.'
body:
• Wildfires raging on the outskirts of Spokane, Washington, have destroyed at least 700 buildings and forced 65,000 people to evacuate, making it the worst natural disaster in the region's history.
  • Three separate blazes — the Old Trails, Fairview, and Autumn Lane fires — have scorched more than 8,000 acres with 0% containment as of Monday.
  • Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency; more than 250,000 acres are burning across the state. President Trump has been briefed.
  • No deaths have been reported, but officials said an unspecified number of people are missing and the toll is expected to change as search teams reach devastated areas.

A City Under Siege

Wildfires burning on the northern fringe of Spokane, Washington, for a third day have destroyed at least 700 buildings and forced roughly 65,000 people to flee their homes in and around the state's second-largest city, officials said Monday.

https://x.com/CBSNews/status/2084424323746673043

The cluster of three blazes — the Old Trails, Fairview, and Autumn Lane fires — ranks as the top firefighting priority in the United States. The fires have scorched more than 8,000 acres since erupting Saturday, driven by temperatures above 100°F and winds gusting to 45 mph. As of Monday, containment remained at 0%.

Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown called it "the worst natural disaster our region has faced." Gent Welsh, adjutant general of the Washington National Guard, said the devastated areas resemble a "war zone."

"This is a nuclear bomb going off in our neighborhoods. This is condensed into where it's demographically a lot of people, so it's really tragic."

— Brent Dallman, Spokane resident, to CNN affiliate KHQ

The Scale of Destruction

Aerial infrared surveys suggest the actual number of damaged or destroyed structures could reach 1,100, with many in residential neighborhoods. Officials cautioned that the figures remain preliminary as crews were still unable to reach some areas due to extreme fire activity.

The fires spread from wooded areas into neighborhoods and commercially developed zones, "turning from a wildfire to an urban conflagration," said Benjamin Cossel, spokesperson for the incident command center. An unspecified number of people have been reported missing.

Major facilities in Spokane have been evacuated, including water reclamation facilities, a waste-to-energy plant, and the Department of Veterans Affairs hospital. At the peak, 60,000 utility customers lost power, according to Avista Utilities.

Statewide Emergency

Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and burn ban on Saturday, banning most recreational and agricultural burning. He authorized additional National Guard soldiers to be deployed after an earlier wildfire-related deployment in July. More than 1,100 firefighters are battling the Spokane-area blazes, part of 29,200 personnel assigned to wildfires nationwide, concentrated in Oregon, Washington, and Idaho.

Ferguson said he spoke with President Trump on Sunday and requested assistance from FEMA. U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell called the response "historic" and said federal officials committed that the Northwest would receive 75% of the nation's firefighting resources.

For the summer so far, about 450,000 acres have burned across Washington state. "This is not normal," said Dave Upthegrove, the state's commissioner of public lands.

Cause Under Investigation

The cause of the fires remains under investigation. The Old Trails Fire started around noon Saturday near Airway Heights and rapidly spread toward the city. After jumping the Spokane River, it triggered Level 3 "go now" evacuation orders across multiple neighborhoods. The Autumn Lane fire, which started south of Suncrest and also jumped the river, was identified as the primary "fire of concern."

The National Weather Service issued a rare Fire Warning for Spokane County — used when active fires are burning in inhabited areas under emergency evacuation orders. Officials warned that high winds and temperatures would persist through the weekend, making firefighting more challenging.

Impact on Spokane's Indian-American Community

Spokane's Indian-American community has grown in recent years, drawn by healthcare jobs at Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center and tech positions at local employers. Several medical facilities are in or near evacuation zones. Community members with family in the affected areas should check the Spokane County evacuation map and register with local shelters if displaced.

No deaths have been reported so far, but officials said "there's a high probability that will change in the coming days" as search teams reach areas that remain inaccessible.
